quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on what the quick GSM rule says, what it assumes and what it is good for.

questions.q: What does GSM stand for?
questions.explain: GSM is grams per square metre, the metric weight of fabric. Weight per square yard is given in ounces (oz/yd²), not grams.

questions.q: In the quick rule, the ends per inch are divided by:
questions.explain: The warp term is EPI ÷ Ne warp and the weft term is PPI ÷ Ne weft; each thread density is divided by its own yarn count. Width does not appear because the result is per square metre.

questions.q: The quick rule assumes a crimp of about 10 % in the yarns.
questions.explain: Yes: the constant 25 includes an allowance of roughly 10 % crimp. A fabric with much more or less crimp will weigh a little more or less than the estimate.

questions.q: Which effect does the quick rule ignore?
questions.explain: The rule ignores width effects (selvedges, width contraction) and uses a fixed crimp allowance. Yarn count and thread density are its inputs, so they are certainly not ignored.

questions.q: How is GSM converted to ounces per square yard?
questions.explain: oz/yd² = GSM ÷ 33.9, e.g. 254 ÷ 33.9 = 7.49. Dividing by 28.35 only converts grams to ounces and forgets that a square yard is smaller than a square metre.

questions.q: Which of these fabrics would normally be the heaviest?
questions.explain: The lecture lists sheeting, poplin, drill and canvas in order of increasing weight; canvas uses coarse yarns set densely and is the heaviest of the four.

questions.q: The exact weight method in Weaving Calculations Lecture 5 adds which factors that the quick rule leaves out?
options: Contraction, width and pounds per linear yard
questions.explain: The exact worksheet allows for contraction, actual width and gives pounds per linear yard, which a costing office needs. Loom speed affects production, not weight.

questions.q: The quick rule can be used directly with tex counts without any conversion.
questions.explain: The rule is written for Ne (indirect) counts, where dividing density by count gives a weight. Tex is a direct count, so a tex value must first be converted to Ne (Ne = 590.5 ÷ tex) or a different formula used.

questions.q: What does the constant 25 in the quick rule represent?
options: The number of picks in a hank
A factor that converts inches, yards and pounds to grams per square metre and includes the crimp allowance
The average width of cloth in inches
The number of ends per dent
questions.explain: The 25 folds together the unit conversions (ends per inch to ends per metre, 840-yd hanks per pound to grams per metre) and the roughly 10 % crimp. It has nothing to do with dents or picks.

questions.q: The lecture says the quick rule is 'close enough' for what purpose?
options: Sorting constructions into sheeting, poplin, drill and canvas
Calculating yarn requirement to the kilogram
questions.explain: It is a classifying estimate, good for telling fabric families apart. For costing and yarn purchase the exact method with contraction and width is needed.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Which way the weight moves when a count or a sett changes, and how GSM and oz/yd² relate.

questions.q: If the picks per inch are increased and nothing else changes, the estimated GSM:
options: Falls, because the cloth becomes thinner
questions.explain: More picks put more weft yarn into every square metre, so the weft term PPI/Ne grows and the weight rises.

questions.q: If the weft count is changed from 16s to 24s Ne with the same picks per inch, the GSM:
options: Falls, because 24s is a finer yarn
questions.explain: Ne is indirect: 24s is finer than 16s, so PPI ÷ 24 is smaller than PPI ÷ 16 and the cloth is lighter. Reading the larger number as the heavier yarn is the classic error.

questions.q: Convert 200 g/m² to ounces per square yard using oz/yd² = GSM ÷ 33.9. Give two decimal places.
Which change leaves the quick GSM estimate exactly the same?
options: Doubling the ends per inch and halving the warp count number
Doubling both the ends per inch and the warp count number
Doubling the picks per inch only
Halving the weft count number only
questions.explain: The warp term is EPI/Ne; doubling both numerator and denominator leaves it unchanged. Doubling EPI while halving Ne multiplies the term by four.

questions.q: Halving the weft count number (for example 20s to 10s) while keeping the same picks per inch doubles the weft term of the quick rule.
questions.explain: PPI ÷ 10 is twice PPI ÷ 20. A 10s yarn is twice as heavy per yard as a 20s yarn, so the same number of picks weighs twice as much.

questions.q: Which expression gives the weight of the warp alone in the quick rule?
questions.explain: The warp contribution is (EPI ÷ Ne warp) × 25. Writing Ne ÷ EPI inverts the fraction and gives a tiny, meaningless number.

questions.q: A square-sett fabric uses the same count N for warp and weft and the same density D for ends and picks. Its quick GSM is:
questions.explain: Both terms equal D/N, so GSM ≈ 2 × (D/N) × 25 = 50 × D/N. Choosing 25 × D/N counts only one of the two thread systems.

questions.q: The lecture's drill is estimated at 254 g/m². What is this in ounces per square yard (÷ 33.9)? Give two decimal places.
questions.explain: 254 ÷ 33.9 = 7.49 oz/yd², the figure shown in the worksheet.

questions.q: A fabric is woven 60" wide and the same construction is then woven 72" wide. According to the quick rule the GSM:
questions.explain: GSM is weight per square metre, so width does not enter the quick rule. Width does change the weight per linear yard, which is where the exact method is needed.

questions.q: Which is the main reason a woven sample may weigh differently from the quick estimate?
options: The actual crimp differs from the assumed 10 %
GSM cannot be measured on cotton
The reed count was not included
questions.explain: The rule's constant assumes about 10 % crimp; a tightly set cloth may crimp much more and weigh more. The reed count affects sett, which is already in EPI.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Apply GSM ≈ (EPI/Ne warp + PPI/Ne weft) × 25 and the 33.9 conversion to typical constructions.

questions.q: Estimate the GSM of a drill 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 with the quick rule. Give one decimal place.
Estimate the GSM of a sheeting 20 × 20 / 60 × 60 with the quick rule.
questions.explain: Each term is 60 ÷ 20 = 3; (3 + 3) × 25 = 150 g/m², the sheeting figure in the worksheet.

questions.q: A sheeting is estimated at 150 g/m². Convert this to ounces per square yard (÷ 33.9), to two decimal places.
Estimate the GSM of a poplin 40 × 40 / 110 × 70 with the quick rule. Give one decimal place.
Estimate the GSM of a canvas 10 × 10 / 60 × 40 with the quick rule.
questions.explain: 60 ÷ 10 = 6; 40 ÷ 10 = 4; (6 + 4) × 25 = 250 g/m². Coarse 10s yarns make it heavy even at a modest sett.

questions.q: Estimate the GSM of 30 × 30 / 120 × 85 with the quick rule. Round to the nearest whole number.
A fabric has a 16s warp at 72 ends per inch and a 12s weft. What picks per inch give a quick-rule GSM of 200? Round to the nearest pick.
questions.explain: 200 ÷ 25 = 8.0 total; warp term 72 ÷ 16 = 4.5; weft term needed 3.5; PPI = 3.5 × 12 = 42 picks per inch.

questions.q: A buyer's specification says 5.04 oz/yd². What is that in g/m²?
questions.explain: GSM = oz/yd² × 33.9 = 5.04 × 33.9 = 170.9 ≈ 171 g/m². 143 is what you get by wrongly multiplying by 28.35 (grams per ounce).

questions.q: A 7.00 oz/yd² denim is quoted. Convert it to g/m² (× 33.9), to one decimal place.
Which of these constructions has the highest quick-rule GSM?
questions.explain: 16 × 12 / 84 × 28 gives (5.25 + 2.33) × 25 ≈ 190 g/m²; the others give 150, 128 and 120. The low pick count is outweighed by the coarse 12s weft and 16s warp.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Using the quick weight rule in the sampling room and the costing office, and knowing when it is not enough.

questions.q: A buyer wants a 7.0 oz/yd² drill. Your proposed 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 estimates at 254 g/m² (7.49 oz/yd²). What is the sensible next step?
options: Accept it — 7.49 is close enough to 7.0
Lighten it, e.g. fewer picks or a finer weft, then re-estimate
Increase the ends per inch to reach 7.0
questions.explain: 7.49 oz is 7 % over the target. Reducing picks or using a finer weft lowers the weft term. More ends or a wider cloth would not reduce weight per square yard.

questions.q: A customer asks for a 150 g/m² sheeting with a 20s warp at 60 ends per inch. Which weft gives the target by the quick rule?
questions.explain: Warp term 60 ÷ 20 = 3; to reach 150 ÷ 25 = 6 the weft term must also be 3, i.e. 60 ÷ 20. A 30s weft at 60 picks gives only 2 (125 g/m²) and a 10s weft gives 6 (225 g/m²).

questions.q: The quick rule gives 171 g/m² but the woven sample weighs 185 g/m². What is the most likely explanation?
options: The actual crimp is higher than the 10 % the rule assumes, so the exact method is needed
GSM cannot be estimated for 30s yarns
questions.explain: A denser or coarser set cloth crimps more than 10 %, putting more yarn into each square metre. The exact method with measured contraction and width explains the difference.

questions.q: The quick GSM rule is accurate enough to fix the final yarn cost per metre in an export quotation.
questions.explain: It is a sorting estimate that ignores width and uses an assumed crimp. For a quotation the exact worksheet with contraction, width and pounds per linear yard should be used.

questions.q: A 400 g/m² canvas inquiry arrives. How should the costing office use the quick rule?
options: As the final weight for the yarn requirement
As a first check that the proposed construction is in the right class, before the exact calculation
Not at all — it only works below 200 g/m²
Only after the fabric is woven
questions.explain: The rule quickly confirms a construction is canvas-weight, after which the exact method sets the yarn requirement. It is not limited to light fabrics; it is simply approximate.

questions.q: Two constructions both estimate at 150 g/m²: 20 × 20 / 60 × 60 and 40 × 40 / 120 × 120. Which gives the finer, smoother sheet?
options: 40 × 40 / 120 × 120, because finer yarns set more closely give a smoother surface at the same weight
They are identical in every way
Neither — equal GSM means equal handle
questions.explain: Same weight does not mean same handle: twice as many threads of half the weight each give a closer, smoother cloth. GSM alone never describes the look and feel.

questions.q: Which list runs from the lightest to the heaviest typical fabric?
questions.explain: Sheeting and poplin are light apparel and bedding cloths; drill is a heavy warp-faced twill and canvas the heaviest. This is the order the lecture uses.

questions.q: A merchandiser converts 254 g/m² for a US buyer by dividing by 28.35 and reports 8.96 oz/yd². Why is this wrong?
options: 28.35 converts grams to ounces but ignores that a square yard is smaller than a square metre; the correct figure is 254 ÷ 33.9 = 7.49
The answer should be multiplied by 28.35
Ounces cannot be used for fabric
questions.explain: A square yard is 0.836 m², so 28.35 ÷ 0.836 = 33.9 is the combined factor. Dividing by 28.35 alone overstates the weight by about 20 %, which could lose the order or the margin.

questions.q: A buyer specifies 4.5 oz/yd². With a 20s warp at 60 ends per inch and a 20s weft, how many picks per inch does the quick rule need? (GSM = oz × 33.9.) Round to the nearest pick.
questions.explain: 4.5 × 33.9 = 152.6 g/m²; ÷ 25 = 6.10; minus warp term 3.0 leaves 3.10; × 20 = 62 picks per inch.

questions.q: Which input mistake would most distort a quick GSM estimate?
options: Entering the width as 64 instead of 63
Entering the warp count as 2 instead of 20
Entering the weave as 2/1 instead of 3/1
questions.explain: The count is a divisor, so 2 instead of 20 multiplies the warp term by ten. Width and weave do not enter the rule and one pick is a tiny change.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step reasoning about crimp, unit conversion, and what GSM does and does not tell you.

questions.q: Why does the quick rule's constant already include crimp?
options: Because yarn in a cloth is longer than the cloth it lies in, so more yarn weight goes into each square metre than the thread count alone suggests
Because crimp makes the yarn thinner
Because the reed stretches the yarn
Because GSM is measured on a crimped sample
questions.explain: Each thread bends over and under the crossing threads, so a metre of cloth contains about 1.1 m of each yarn; the constant 25 is scaled up for this. Crimp does not change the yarn's count.

questions.q: Suppose the constant 25 is taken as 22.7 × 1.10 (yarn weight without crimp × a 10 % crimp allowance). What would the drill 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 weigh if there were no crimp at all? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: (6.40 + 3.75) × 22.7 = 230.4 g/m², about 23 g/m² less than the 253.75 with crimp included. Crimp is a real part of fabric weight.

questions.q: A student writes GSM ≈ (Ne warp ÷ EPI + Ne weft ÷ PPI) × 25 and gets about 11 g/m² for a drill. What went wrong?
options: The fractions are inverted — density must be divided by count, not count by density
The warp and weft terms should be multiplied
questions.explain: (20 ÷ 128 + 16 ÷ 60) × 25 ≈ 11, absurd for a drill. The correct form (128 ÷ 20 + 60 ÷ 16) × 25 ≈ 254 g/m². An answer that is impossible for the fabric class is the signal to check the formula.

questions.q: For the drill 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 the warp term is 6.40 and the weft term 3.75. What percentage of the fabric weight is weft? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: Weft share = 3.75 ÷ 10.15 = 0.369, i.e. 36.9 %. The warp carries the other 63.1 %, as expected for a warp-faced drill.

questions.q: Two fabrics with the same GSM must have the same cover and the same handle.
questions.explain: GSM is only weight per area. A cloth of fine yarns set closely and one of coarse yarns set openly can weigh the same yet look and feel completely different.

questions.q: The worksheet shows 5.04 oz/yd² for a fabric. Working back, what GSM did the quick rule give?
questions.explain: GSM = 5.04 × 33.9 = 170.9 ≈ 171 g/m², the 'Your fabric' column. 143 comes from the wrong factor 28.35.

questions.q: A 40s warp is set at 120 ends per inch and the weft is 30s. What is the maximum picks per inch that keeps the quick-rule GSM at or below 140? Round down to a whole pick.
questions.explain: 140 ÷ 25 = 5.6; warp term 120 ÷ 40 = 3.0; weft term allowed 2.6; PPI = 2.6 × 30 = 78 picks per inch.

questions.q: Why does the width of the cloth not appear in the GSM formula, yet matter to the costing office?
options: Because GSM is per square metre, but the price and yarn requirement are per linear metre or yard, which depend on width
Because width only affects the warp count
Because width is included in the picks per inch
questions.explain: Weight per unit area is independent of width, but a wider cloth has more ends and longer picks, so weight and cost per linear yard rise. That is why the exact method asks for width.

questions.q: A 254 g/m² cloth is 63 inches (1.60 m) wide. Roughly what does one linear yard (0.914 m) weigh? (1 lb = 453.6 g.)
questions.explain: Area of one linear yard = 1.60 × 0.914 = 1.463 m²; × 254 = 371.6 g; ÷ 453.6 = 0.82 lb. This is the 'pounds per linear yard' the exact worksheet produces.

questions.q: A weft is specified as 59 tex. Before using the quick rule you convert it to Ne (Ne = 590.5 ÷ tex). What value do you use?
questions.explain: 590.5 ÷ 59 ≈ 10, so the weft is a 10s yarn. Using 59 directly would make a coarse yarn look like a fine one and understate the weight nearly six-fold.
